html:
The Fortress of Luxembourg grew from a small castle on the Bock rock that Count Siegfried acquired in 963. The town, and later the country, grew up around it.

For eight centuries Burgundians, Spaniards, French, Austrians and Prussians each held and strengthened it. After Louis XIV took it in 1684, his engineer Vauban rebuilt it. Rings of walls and tunnels cut into the rock, the casemates, earned it the name Gibraltar of the North.

The Treaty of London of 1867 made Luxembourg neutral and had most of the walls pulled down. The old quarter and what is left of the fortifications are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
